title: Data Transformation, Mapping, and Formatting
summary: The single most common real-world automation problem is that data from one system never quite matches what the next system expects, so data transformation is a core, everyday skill. Field mapping is the basic act of connecting the output of one step
content:
# Data Transformation, Mapping, and Formatting ##### The 90% of the job nobody puts in the tutorial Watch any automation demo and it looks effortless: drag the `email` field from the trigger into the `email` field of the action. Done. Now build one for a real client. The form calls it `Email Address`; the CRM wants `email`. The name arrives as one field, `"ananya rao"`, and the CRM needs `firstname` and `lastname`, properly capitalized. The date says `05/01/2024` — which could be 5 January or 1 May, and you genuinely cannot tell. The price is the string `"$1,299.00"` and the accounting system wants the number `1299.0`. The country is `"india"`, `"IN"`, `"India "` or `"Bharat"` depending on who typed it. Research on data preparation consistently finds that practitioners spend the majority of their time on exactly this — cleaning and reshaping data before anything interesting happens (Terrizzano et al., 2015, memorably call it the journey "from the wild to the lake"). Automation is no different. **Transformation is not a side task; it is the job.** ##### Field mapping between different schemas A **schema** is the shape of a record: which fields exist, what they are named, what types they hold. Two systems almost never share one. Mapping is the act of declaring correspondence. Do it deliberately, as a document, before you touch a tool: ```text SOURCE (Google Form) TRANSFORM TARGET (HubSpot) ───────────────────────── ────────────────────────── ───────────────── Email Address → lowercase, trim → email Full Name → split on first space, capitalize each part → firstname / lastname Company → trim → company Phone → strip non-digits, +91 → phone Team Size ("45") → to number → numemployees Submitted (UTC ISO) → to Asia/Kolkata date → createdate (none) → constant "website_form" → lead_source ``` Four mapping situations recur, and naming them helps: - **One-to-one** — `email` → `email`. Rare and delightful. - **One-to-many** — one `Full Name` splits into two fields. - **Many-to-one** — `address_line1` + `city` + `pin` concatenate into one `address` string. - **Constant / derived** — a value not in the source at all: a source tag, a computed tier, a timestamp. Write this table down first. Half of all "why is this field empty?" debugging comes from mapping that was improvised at 11 p.m. ##### Text operations The workhorses, available in Zapier Formatter, Make functions, and n8n expressions alike: - **trim** — remove leading/trailing whitespace. Apply to *everything* from a form. Invisible spaces break exact-match lookups constantly. - **lowercase / uppercase / capitalize** — normalize emails to lowercase, country codes to uppercase, names to title case. - **split** — `"ananya rao"` → `["ananya", "rao"]`. - **join** — the reverse, with a separator. - **replace** — remove commas from numbers, strip currency symbols, fix known typos. - **substring / truncate** — fit a 500-character message into a 140-character field. - **regex extract** — pull an email, a URL, an order ID or a number out of free text. - **default** — substitute a fallback when a value is empty. Here is a complete cleaning routine in an n8n Code node, handling the messy record from today's practical task: ```javascript // Input: { full_name: " ananya RAO ", date: "05/01/2024", // price: "$1,299.00", country: "india", phone: "98765 43210" } // Output: a clean, typed, consistently shaped record. const out = []; for (const item of $input.all()) { const r = item.json; // --- Name: collapse whitespace, split, title-case --- const clean = (r.full_name ?? '').replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim(); const parts = clean.split(' '); const title = (s) => s ? s[0].toUpperCase() + s.slice(1).toLowerCase() : ''; const firstName = title(parts[0] ?? ''); const lastName = parts.slice(1).map(title).join(' '); // --- Date: DD/MM/YYYY -> ISO 8601 (documented assumption!) --- const [d, m, y] = (r.date ?? '').split('/'); const isoDate = (d && m && y) ? `${y}-${m.padStart(2, '0')}-${d.padStart(2, '0')}` : null; // --- Price: strip currency symbol and thousands separators --- const priceNum = Number(String(r.price ?? '').replace(/[^0-9.\-]/g, '')); // --- Phone: digits only, force +91 country code --- const digits = String(r.phone ?? '').replace(/\D/g, ''); const phone = digits.length === 10 ? `+91${digits}` : digits.startsWith('91') ? `+${digits}` : digits ? `+${digits}` : null; out.push({ json: { first_name: firstName, last_name: lastName, order_date: isoDate, price: Number.isFinite(priceNum) ? priceNum : null, currency: 'INR', phone, country_code: (r.country ?? '').trim().slice(0, 2).toUpperCase(), clean_ok: Boolean(firstName && isoDate && Number.isFinite(priceNum)), }, }); } return out; ``` Two things to steal from this code. The `clean_ok` flag lets a downstream filter route bad records to a human instead of writing garbage. And every conversion has a **fallback** (`?? ''`, `null`), so a missing field produces a null rather than crashing the whole run. ##### Numbers and currency Numbers arrive as strings surprisingly often — from forms, from CSVs, from APIs that quote everything. The conversion rules: - **Strip before converting.** Remove currency symbols, thousands separators, and stray spaces. `Number("₹1,299.00")` is `NaN`; `Number("1299.00")` is `1299`. - **Beware locale separators.** `1.299,00` is one thousand two hundred ninety-nine in German notation. In Indian formatting, `12,34,567` uses lakh grouping, not thousands. Know your source's convention. - **Store raw numbers, format only for display.** Your database column should hold `1299`, not `"₹1,299.00"`. Formatting is a presentation concern applied at the last step — in the email body, not in the record. - **Watch floating point.** `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` in JavaScript. For money, work in the smallest unit (paise, cents) as integers, or round explicitly at the end: `Math.round(x * 100) / 100`. - **Percentages are ambiguous.** Is `18` eighteen percent or 1800%? Decide and document. ##### Dates, times, and time zones This is the category that causes the most production bugs, which is why the assignment asks for a troubleshooting guide on it. **Why the problems happen:** 1. **Ambiguous formats.** `05/01/2024` is 5 January in India and the UK, 1 May in the US. There is no way to know from the value alone — you must know the source. 2. **Missing time zone.** `2026-03-14T09:12:44` with no offset is meaningless. Is that UTC or IST? A 5.5-hour error is one interpretation away. 3. **Silent conversion.** Every tool has a default time zone (often UTC). Your workflow, your account, the source app and the destination app may each have a different one, and each hop can shift the value. 4. **Date-only values.** A "date" with no time is often stored as midnight UTC, which in IST is 5:30 a.m. *the same day* — but in US Pacific is 4 p.m. *the previous day*. This is how birthdays end up off by one. 5. **DST.** Not an issue for Asia/Kolkata, but very much one when your client is in New York or London, and it shifts twice a year. **Three practices that prevent almost all of it:** - **Normalize to ISO 8601 with an explicit offset the moment data enters.** `2026-03-14T09:12:44+05:30`. Unambiguous, sortable as text, universally parseable. - **Store in UTC, display in local.** Keep one canonical representation internally; convert only at the boundary where a human reads it. - **Set the time zone explicitly everywhere** — the Zapier Zap settings, the Make organization, n8n's `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, and every Calendar event's `timeZone` field. Never rely on a default. A fourth, practical one: when parsing an ambiguous date, **test with a day above 12**. If `13/01/2024` parses successfully and `01/13/2024` fails, you have proven the source uses DD/MM. ##### Building and restructuring JSON payloads Often the target API wants a structure quite unlike your flat input — nested objects, arrays of line items, specific wrappers. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Flat source record] --> B[Clean & type
text, number, date ops] B --> C[Rename to target
field names] C --> D[Nest & group
build objects/arrays] D --> E[Validate
required fields present?] E -->|ok| F[Send to API] E -->|fail| G[Route to error log] ``` The professional habit is to make the final shape **explicit** rather than assembled implicitly across a dozen mapped boxes. In n8n use a **Set node with "Keep Only Set"**; in Make, build the JSON in a single field with inline functions; in Zapier, use Code by Zapier for anything nested. Then the workflow itself documents the contract: ```json { "customer": { "first_name": "Ananya", "last_name": "Rao", "email": "ananya@example.com", "phone": "+919876543210" }, "order": { "date": "2024-01-05", "currency": "INR", "total": 1299.00, "items": [ { "sku": "KB-01", "qty": 1, "unit_price": 1299.00 } ] }, "meta": { "source": "website_form", "country_code": "IN" } } ``` If you work from a terminal, `jq` is the standard tool for exactly this kind of reshaping and is worth twenty minutes of your time — `jq '{name: .full_name, total: (.price|tonumber)}'` is a whole transformation in one line. ##### Common pitfalls - **Not trimming.** `"ananya@example.com "` never matches in a lookup. - **Assuming a date format** instead of confirming it with the source. - **Formatting numbers too early**, then trying to do arithmetic on `"₹1,299.00"`. - **Splitting names naively.** "Dr. Ananya Rao Deshmukh" and "Ananya" (single word) both break `parts[0]/parts[1]` logic. Handle the one-word and multi-part cases. - **No null handling** — one missing field crashes the whole run instead of one record. - **Transforming the same value repeatedly** across steps instead of once, early. - **Silent type coercion** — `"9" > "10"` is `true` in string comparison. - **Losing the original.** Always keep the raw payload somewhere; when a transformation turns out to be wrong, you need the source to reprocess. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is the messy record: full name in one field, a date like `05/01/2024`, a price like `$1,299.00`. Build a flow that **splits the name, reformats the date to ISO, and converts the price to a clean number**. Then deliberately feed it edge cases — a single-word name, an empty price, a date of `13/01/2024` — and see what breaks. That is the real lesson. The mini project is the **data normalizer**: accept records from *two differently-structured sources* and output them in one consistent JSON schema, with standardized field names, ISO dates, numeric prices, and uppercase country codes. Write the mapping table for both sources first. This pattern — many messy inputs, one clean canonical shape — is exactly what integration work looks like professionally. For the assignment, write your **date/time-zone troubleshooting guide**: why the problems happen (ambiguous formats, missing offsets, differing defaults, date-only midnight, DST) and three practices to avoid them (ISO 8601 with offset at ingestion, UTC storage with local display, explicit time zone configuration everywhere). Add the "test with a day above 12" trick — it is the kind of concrete tip that marks real experience. ##### Key takeaways - Transformation is the bulk of real automation work; write your source-to-target mapping table before building. - Trim and normalize every text value on entry — invisible whitespace and case differences silently break lookups. - Convert strings to real numbers by stripping symbols first; store raw values and format only for display, using integers for money. - Dates are the top source of production bugs: normalize to ISO 8601 with an offset, store UTC, display local, and set time zones explicitly. - Build the target payload explicitly in one place, validate required fields, keep the raw input, and flag bad records instead of writing them.
